title: Warm Climates May Have Helped Crocodile Kin Outlast the Dinosaurs
paragraphs: When an asteroid struck Earth some 66 million years ago, most dinosaurs vanished, but crocodiles and their kin pulled through. A study led by University College London, published in Science Advances, contends that an enduring attachment to warm climates may have been what spared them.

The team drew on more than 7,000 fossils and records spanning over 400 living and extinct species, reconstructed the temperatures and rainfall each preferred, and set the results against climate and geography simulations covering 245 million years. When the simulated aftermath included a 5% or 10% fall in sunlight owing to dust and ash, warm belts around the equator stayed habitable for crocodile relatives; a 15% fall left almost nowhere suitable, though the authors regard that as improbable. Earlier modelling by the same group had found that the habitats open to non-avian dinosaurs contracted far more severely.

As ever with palaeontological modelling, caveats abound. The refuges are inferred rather than observed, and the authors themselves stress that warmth was probably one factor among many, with small size, a semi-aquatic way of life, adaptable diets and low energy demands also playing a part. They add that roads, farms and cities could now hinder crocodiles from following suitable climates as the planet warms. The research was funded by the Royal Society, the Leverhulme Trust and the Natural Environment Research Council.

questions.q: What did the study conclude may have spared crocodile relatives?
How did the authors view a 15% fall in sunlight?
What modern concern do the authors raise?
questions.a: Human land use may stop crocodiles from following suitable climates.
